output.headline: Police arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas over Channel dinghy slashing
output.bodyHtml:
Police have arrested Daniel Thomas, the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist, on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, two days after he filmed himself slashing the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was on board.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said in a statement that a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, had been arrested on Wednesday night “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety under section 11 of the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990”.

Officers said Thomas was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals under section 58 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995”.

Thomas appears to have filmed his own arrest on Wednesday night, and a video was uploaded to his YouTube channel showing the moment, apparently at a garage. An officer told him he had been “involved in criminal damage that has recklessly endangered someone’s life”.

Thomas, who prefers to go by the name Danny Tommo, said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

Over the summer Thomas brought together dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella movement Patriot Platform.

He was behind anti-immigration marches by masked men this month in Dover and Portsmouth.

More details soon …
output.standfirst: Police have arrested the 37-year-old on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life

output.headline: Andy Burnham signals he could lift ban on alcohol in football stands
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, saying it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.

The prime minister, a committed Everton fan who still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.

The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, though police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.

Burnham has long argued against the ban, calling it discriminatory and out of date, a hangover from an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.

Asked by reporters on the plane to New York about lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.

“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.

The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.

A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.

“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”

A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”

Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.

Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.
output.standfirst: Prime minister argues alcohol ban on football fans is discriminatory when supporters of other sports face no such restriction

output.headline: Research reveals millions in England unaware they have ‘silent killer’ condition
output.bodyHtml:
Research reveals the scale of high blood pressure in England: millions of people are unaware they have the ‘silent killer’ condition, and only half of those being treated by a GP have it under control.

The largest ever study of its kind found that most people with hypertension – 59 per cent – are undiagnosed, leaving them at greater risk of stroke, heart attack and early death.

Among those who are diagnosed and receiving medication from their family doctor, the Oxford University study of 1.4 million adults suggests blood pressure remains out of control in 50 per cent of cases.

Researchers said the findings, published in journal BMJ Public Health, suggested the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure in England was ‘not fit for purpose’.

The study drew on data from the Our Future Health programme and looked at people enrolled between 2022 and 2025 with high blood pressure, defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher.

Related: ‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts say

Researchers calculated that more than a third of adults (37 per cent) had high blood pressure, with six in 10 of these unaware of their condition.

Hypertension was almost 50 per cent more common in men than women (42 per cent compared with 29 per cent across all ages), and more common in older people, according to the research.

The researchers pointed to substantial improvements in high blood pressure detection and control during the 2000s, though progress has plateaued since about 2011.

There were also ‘indications of worsening trends following the Covid-19 pandemic, possibly because disruptions to healthcare delivery may have had lasting effects’.

Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician at Oxford Population Health and lead author of the study, said: ‘While hypertension is largely a “silent killer”, the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure is not fit for purpose.

‘Our study highlights the prevalence of hypertension across demographics. This underscores the need for population-wide prevention strategies alongside targeted treatment for people at high cardiovascular risk.’

The researchers said ‘the most striking finding’ of the study was the high absolute number and proportion of people with undiagnosed hypertension, while only half of adults with high blood pressure treated by a GP were adequately controlled.

Dr Iain Turnbull, a GP, deputy chief medical officer at Our Future Health and a clinical research fellow at Oxford Population Health, said it was not clear why 50 per cent of patients who said they were taking blood pressure-lowering drugs had uncontrolled hypertension.

‘Blood pressure varies considerably between people, and some people need changes in dose or two or more different medicines before it is brought under control. Other health conditions and medications can affect blood pressure, too.

Related: AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggests

‘There are also practical and social factors: side effects, complicated treatment regimens and competing health or life pressures can make medicines difficult to take consistently. Weight, diet, salt intake, alcohol and physical activity can also influence blood pressure.

‘So a high reading can have many explanations and shouldn’t be seen simply as a reflection of what an individual patient or healthcare professional has done.

‘There are also some important caveats … we did not have prescribing records available to independently confirm medication use, and a blood pressure measurement on one day does not necessarily represent someone’s usual blood pressure.

‘Even with those caveats, I wouldn’t regard 50 per cent as a satisfactory figure. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, and bringing it under control reduces that risk.’

Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, said the study ‘paints a concerning picture of the scale of undetected high blood pressure in the UK, and the challenges of keeping blood pressure under control in those already receiving treatment’.

‘Better detection and treatment could help tens of thousands of people to avoid a preventable heart attack and stroke,’ he added. ‘But to achieve this, we will need to rethink how we identify, treat and support those at risk so that blood pressure checks and effective treatment can benefit everyone.’
output.standfirst: Researchers say approach to detecting high blood pressure in England is ‘not fit for purpose’, with 59 per cent of cases undiagnosed

output.headline: Judge orders Trump administration to restore White House access for CNN, MS Now and Politico
output.bodyHtml:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to temporarily restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, ruling that the president’s ban on the three outlets was likely unconstitutional.

US district judge Tim Kelly issued the order in a lawsuit that the news organisations filed contesting the ban, which the president had announced on 18 September.

Kelly ordered the administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and issued a temporary restraining order that will remain in effect for 14 days. Orders of this kind are typically designed to preserve the status quo while the court carries out a closer review of the case.

Related: DoJ defends Trump media ban: ‘Access to the White House is a privilege’

Earlier on Wednesday, Kelly had cited past case law that clearly set out the need for a distinct process, involving advance notice of an infraction and the opportunity to plead one’s case.

The judge said that prior cases made clear that ‘before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard’.

A Justice Department lawyer told the judge that the administration had given a sufficient explanation for revoking the press passes, in letters sent to the news outlets on Tuesday. But the judge signalled scepticism of that argument, noting that the letters had been sent after the revocation took place and after the lawsuit was filed.

Trump had said on social media that the three outlets ‘shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES’, while justice department lawyers sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, arguing that the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They asked for a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge continues.

In a legal filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president has the authority to suspend access for news organisations.

A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations filed a legal brief on Wednesday backing the three outlets. They asserted that ‘stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of supreme court jurisprudence’.

The brief was signed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.

With Reuters and the Associated Press
output.standfirst: A federal judge orders the temporary restoration of White House access for the three media outlets, ruling that Donald Trump's ban on them was likely unconstitutional

output.headline: UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer
output.bodyHtml:
The UK has told countries around the world that the climate and nature crises, together with the coming El Niño, threaten their national security and defence, sharing the findings of a report that was suppressed under Keir Starmer.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, presented the findings to foreign ministers from the EU, Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night, at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, drawing on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs which found that the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.

Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that the coming El Niño, supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before.

“We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.”

This year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation showed governments what lies ahead, he said, and must be addressed at the highest levels.

“Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.”

With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband set out research showing that the collapse of global ecosystems such as in the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would affect national security around the world.

The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, had been due to be published last October, but was suppressed by Downing Street on the eve of its launch. A redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act, though ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public.

Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian that governments should treat the climate as they would any other threat to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states.

“If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.”

He said it was unsurprising that the JIC report was suppressed and redacted, since it was “very rare” for security reports to be published.

Miliband is to appoint a new special representative for climate security, along with a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, bringing together military and security experts with climate scientists.

He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, which will go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries.

The closed-door meeting among foreign ministers followed a public speech Miliband gave on Monday at the UN general assembly, which touched on the links between climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he intended to put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy.

On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit.

“Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.”

He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.”

Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments.

“But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”
output.standfirst: Ed Miliband tells foreign ministers from the EU, Kenya and other countries that the coming El Niño poses a critical threat to national defences

output.headline: Netanyahu delivers defiant UN speech as he faces protests and political isolation
output.bodyHtml:
Benjamin Netanyahu takes the stage at the UN on Thursday to deliver a familiar message of defiance, even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader increasingly isolated.

He is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades, with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

Israel is facing growing condemnation internationally. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.

The US, meanwhile, is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel: 62 per cent of respondents told Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60 per cent of American Jews in a poll released this week said they hoped he would be voted out in October.

Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal, telling demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech, casting criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.

“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”

“At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added.

Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.

“Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action.

She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”

Palestinian representatives, meanwhile, are calling on diplomatic missions to send staff for a planned walkout during Netanyahu’s speech, to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

In Danon’s telling, though, Israel’s problem is largely one of public relations rather than of policy: he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the sharp shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to set out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?”

He did not elaborate on those specific measures ahead of the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening closely as they calibrate their message to voters – and to the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also at his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”

Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason for heading home quickly after the speech.

A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit, but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.

With criticism coming from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading Democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign fought between two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support it has enjoyed in the past.

Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.

Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”

Multiple flashpoints remain, though, for anger from both US political parties as well as the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.

Asked whether a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, pointing to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not happen, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”

He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism, led by the UK, over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction that would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement. Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.

The protests, in fact, began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York.

On Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport, protesting against weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft.

Aber Kawas, who in November is set to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers in protesting against Netanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.

“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.

Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.
output.standfirst: Prime minister says he will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he faces his toughest re-election challenge yet

output.headline: Nick Clegg dismisses fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity
output.bodyHtml:
Nick Clegg has played down fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, casting the idea as a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”.

The former UK deputy prime minister said tech bosses should focus on addressing known “specific threats” such as cybersecurity, bio-weapons and emotional dependence, rather than dwelling on what he called the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.

In an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he said: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”

Clegg, who was formerly president of global affairs at Meta, owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre company, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs, said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry.

“They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said, noting that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”.

“There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things,” he added.

Asked about the autonomous hack carried out by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face, Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency”.

However, he said this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration, given its competitive approach to AI. He also suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed there as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.

He added: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”

Asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, Clegg noted that the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”

Clegg also disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable, or producing only closed models, where the source code is not made public, which he said the evidence showed were no safer than open-source models.

Instead, he suggested: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”
output.standfirst:
Former deputy prime minister, now working in tech, says much of the sector is ‘winding themselves up into a lather’

  • UK politics live – latest updates

output.headline: Trump greets Xi Jinping on arrival in rare gesture as US-China trade truce is extended
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump greeted Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, taking the unusual step of welcoming the Chinese leader in person as his state visit to Washington began.

The ceremony laid on for Xi’s arrival was lavish: a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers, and the flags and national anthems of both countries presented in turn.

US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and the first lady, Melania, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, in person on Wednesday evening.

Related: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China

Xi’s visit comes as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations general assembly, though the Chinese leader will not address the meeting; he has attended the UNGA only once since becoming president in 2012.

“It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters. “I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced on Wednesday that the US and China had agreed to extend the so-called Busan agreement, the temporary truce that has paused hostilities in the trade war between the world’s two biggest economies.

Bessent, who met the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News that the agreement would run until 10 January, two months beyond its original expiry date.

The pageantry continues with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other events planned for the visit.

The simmering trade war is one of several thorny issues Trump and Xi are due to discuss over the two-day visit, alongside the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability.

The White House has invited major tech leaders, including executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday.

One moment broke from the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony: Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed Trump recoiling at the flyover while Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men.

The moment, widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but did not appear in the edited highlights of the ceremony that Trump’s aides released later.

The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, and the race to advance AI has become a major topic among tech companies, especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, and is instead pressing for greater investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically, raising the stakes further for both the US and China.

Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the welcome Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

Robert Mackey contributed reporting
output.standfirst:
President lays out the red carpet for Xi Jinping as the treasury secretary announces an extension of the ‘Busan agreement’ pausing trade war hostilities
